messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 77
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Politician
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
- Pcl5: 42

# Vignette: Amara

Amara is a 77-year-old African woman who has spent the better part of four decades in public life. She sits in the regional assembly as a senior legislator, known to colleagues and constituents alike for her measured voice and her unwillingness to be interrupted. What very few people know — what she has protected as carefully as she has protected her public reputation — is that for eleven years, between the ages of thirty-one and forty-two, her first husband beat her.

It began gradually, the way she now understands these things often do. A shove after a disagreement. A slap that was followed by tears and flowers. By the time the violence became regular and severe — fists, a belt, once a ceramic lamp broken across her back — she had already learned to arrange her schedule around his moods, to wear certain fabrics, to make sure she was never the last one laughing. She left him only after he fractured two of her ribs during an argument about a constituency meeting she had attended without his permission. She packed a single bag and drove herself to her sister's house, and she never went back.

She has been married to her second husband, a retired physician, for thirty-one years. By any external measure, her life since leaving is a story of remarkable resilience. She raised three children, built a legislative career, and has been celebrated at national women's conferences as a symbol of strength. She accepted those tributes graciously and believed, for a long time, that she had simply moved on.

Then, two years ago, a junior female colleague disclosed to the assembly that her own partner had been abusing her. Amara was asked to lead the parliamentary response. She agreed immediately, because of course she did — it was the right thing, the necessary thing. But sitting in the chamber during the first formal hearing, listening to the younger woman describe the particular sound of a door being locked from the inside, something in Amara came loose. She drove home that evening and sat in her car in the driveway for two hours, unable to explain to herself why she could not open the door.

Since then, sleep has become unreliable and hostile. She wakes most nights between two and four in the morning with her heart already pounding, the details of dreams she cannot fully recall leaving a residue of dread that takes hours to lift. During assembly sessions, if a male colleague raises his voice sharply or moves his chair suddenly, she feels a jolt of fear so physical it embarrasses her — a tightening in her chest, a narrowing of her vision, the impulse to become very still and very small. She finds this intolerable. She is not, she tells herself, a woman who becomes small.

She has begun avoiding certain corridors in the assembly building, certain colleagues whose mannerisms remind her of nothing she can name precisely. She has stopped attending the women's advocacy dinners she once chaired. When her husband reaches across the bed in the night, she sometimes flinches before she can stop herself, and she watches him absorb that with a quiet sadness that she finds harder to bear than the flinching itself.

She describes her emotional life in the present tense as "flat most of the time, and then suddenly not." She is irritable with her staff in ways that are new and that she notices with dismay. She has difficulty reading legislation she has been reading for decades, finding that her attention slides away from the page. She feels, she says — choosing the word carefully, as she chooses all her words — hollowed. As though something that had been sealed for a long time has been opened, and what was inside was not the nothing she had assumed, but something that had been waiting with considerable patience.

She is 77 years old. She has survived a great deal. She is not entirely sure what it means that this is happening now.
